sections.h2: What is the Maine homestead exemption and how much does it take off?
sections.html:
The Maine homestead exemption lowers the taxable value of your permanent home by up to $25,000. The Maine Revenue Services program FAQ says the amount is adjusted by the local certified ratio, so a town with an 80% ratio gives an exemption of $20,000. The exemption cannot be larger than the value of the homestead itself.

Under 36 M.R.S. §683 the $25,000 is built from two pieces: $10,000 of just value in the base subsection, plus an additional $15,000 for tax years beginning on or after April 1, 2020. It sits on top of other exemptions that a homeowner may already hold, such as the ones in sections 653 and 654-A. It is not a credit on the bill. It shrinks the value the town multiplies by its tax rate.

For a seller, the practical point is simple. The exemption is attached to a person who lives in the house, not to the house forever. When ownership or residence changes, the break stops, and the next owner has to qualify on their own.

sections.h2: Who qualifies for the Maine homestead exemption?
sections.html:
You qualify if you are a permanent Maine resident, the home is your permanent residence, and you have owned a home in Maine for the twelve months before you apply. Those three tests come from the Maine Revenue Services Homestead Exemption Program FAQ and from the statute.

  • Camps, vacation homes and second residences do not count. You can have only one permanent residence at a time.
  • The home must be residential property assessed as real property. A mobile home on a rented lot may qualify.
  • Permanent residence is presumed to continue until circumstances show otherwise. The test is whether you intend to return when you are away.
  • There is no income limit. A task force report covered by the press notes that the exemption is open to permanent-resident homeowners, not renters.
  • If the home has several owners, only one signature is required on the application. The exemption can be divided among co-owners who live there in proportion to their interests.

A person who loses a homestead to tax lien foreclosure and later gets it back from the municipality is treated as having owned it the whole time, and the town's brief ownership does not disqualify them.

sections.h2: How and when do you file for the exemption in Maine?
sections.html:
You file a written application with your municipal assessor on or before April 1. A form filed after April 1 applies to the next year's assessment, so a late application costs a full tax year of savings.

Most towns hand out the form, and Maine Revenue Services also posts it on its property tax forms page. The program FAQ gives two answers about where to file: one says the municipality where the property is located and another says the municipality where you reside. For a normal owner-occupied house those are the same town, so call the assessor if yours is not.

You do not have to renew every year. The exemption stays in place as long as ownership and residency stay the same. If an assessor denies the application, the notice must give reasons, and the owner may appeal in writing to the local Board of Assessment Review or the county commissioners. Maine Revenue Services Property Tax Bulletin No. 10 adds that denials of homestead, veteran and blind exemptions can go through the abatement process.

The old section 683 states that its exemptions are discontinued for property tax years beginning on or after April 1, 2027, and a new section, 36 M.R.S. §683-A, takes over from that date. Maine Revenue Services says the base homestead exemption stays at $25,000 of just value under the new section, and that veteran and blind exemptions are added to the same statute.

The Maine Revenue Services slides say applications for the higher amounts must be made to the local assessor before April 1, 2027. The 2027 figures also get multiplied by the local certified ratio. Both statutes tie the exemption to a permanent resident who has owned the homestead for the preceding 12 months.

sections.h2: How big is the program statewide?
sections.html:
Maine towns reported 325,426 homestead exemptions worth $7,410,258,960 in the 2025 Municipal Valuation Return, according to the Maine Revenue Services statistical summary.

Under current law the state reimburses 76% of the taxes lost to the exemption and municipalities absorb the rest. The task force recommended full reimbursement for any increase in the amount.

sections.h2: Does the homestead exemption affect selling a house in Maine?
sections.html:
Yes, in a quiet way: it affects who owes what in the year of the sale, and it can change what a buyer pays next year. Maine taxes what you own on April 1, and the tax year runs April 1 to March 31 under 36 M.R.S. §502.

Closing usually involves a proration. Under §558 a buyer and seller may agree to split property tax pro rata over the municipality's fiscal year unless they agree on a different period. Since the bill already reflects your exemption for that year, the proration uses the lower number.

A buyer does not inherit your exemption. If the buyer will live in the house, they file their own application by April 1 and the town applies it to the next assessment. A buyer who cannot meet the twelve-month ownership test, or who plans to rent the house out, may not get the same bill you did.. Mention that to a buyer who is looking only at your old tax bill.

The state also charges a real estate transfer tax of $2.20 per $500 of value, split equally between buyer and seller under §4641-A. On a $300,000 sale that is $660 for each side.

sections.h2: What if you inherit a house that had a homestead exemption?
sections.html:
An inherited house that no one lives in will usually not keep the exemption, because the exemption rests on the owner using the home as a permanent residence. The FAQ says the break stays in effect only while ownership and residency are unchanged, and it does not spell out what to report after a death, so ask the assessor how the town handles it.

Heirs who plan to sell should look at the April 1 date. If the owner died after April 1 and the exemption was in place that day, the town has already set that year's bill. If the house sits vacant into the next tax year, expect a full bill with no exemption. Our Maine probate guide explains who has the authority to sell the property.

sections.h2: Does the state deferral program affect a sale?
sections.html: The State Property Tax Deferral Program is the one that matters most at closing. To qualify, you must be 65 or older or unable to work due to permanent disability, with household income under $80,000 and liquid assets under $100,000 ($150,000 with multiple owners). The state pays the tax, then places a lien on the home. Selling or transferring the home requires repayment of all deferred taxes, interest and costs. If you are leaving the program because of a sale, the payoff comes out of your proceeds.

sections.h2: Which sellers should check their homestead status before listing?
sections.html:
• Owners who moved out and are renting the house. The home is no longer the permanent residence, so the exemption may have ended.
  • Owners who bought a second Maine home in the last year. You can have only one permanent residence.
  • Heirs holding a vacant house. Ownership has changed and residence has stopped.
  • Owners with a deferral lien. Expect a payoff figure from Maine Revenue Services at closing.

If any of these describes you and the house needs work you cannot afford before a sale, a direct sale to a cash buyer can simplify the tax side because there is no buyer financing or inspection renegotiation holding up the proration. That is the kind of situation Cash Home Buyers works with, and we do not promise a price until we see the property.

faqs.q: Is the Maine homestead exemption still $25,000?
faqs.a: Yes. Maine Revenue Services lists the exemption at up to $25,000 of just value as of April 1, 2026, and says the base stays at $25,000 under the new section starting April 1, 2027. The amount is multiplied by your town's certified ratio.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to apply?
faqs.a: April 1. A form filed after April 1 applies to the next year's assessment, and the application goes to your municipal assessor.

faqs.q: Do I have to reapply every year?
faqs.a: No. The exemption stays in effect as long as ownership and residency do not change, according to the Maine Revenue Services FAQ.

faqs.q: Does the buyer get my homestead exemption when I sell?
faqs.a: No. The exemption belongs to the permanent resident who owns and lives in the home. A buyer who will live there files their own application by April 1.

faqs.q: Can I get the exemption on a camp or second home?
faqs.a: No. Camps, vacation homes and second residences do not qualify, and you can have only one permanent residence at a time.

faqs.q: What if the assessor denies my homestead application?
faqs.a: You may appeal in writing to the local Board of Assessment Review or the county commissioners, and Property Tax Bulletin No. 10 notes that exemption denials can go through the abatement process.
The old section 683 is discontinued for tax years beginning April 1, 2027, but section 683-A takes over with a base exemption of up to $25,000, plus veteran and blind exemptions.
